title: Cindy: How to Pace 20 Minutes of Bodyweight Work
excerpt: Five pull-ups, ten push-ups, fifteen air squats, twenty minutes. How to pick a round pace you can hold, where rounds actually get lost, and how to scale Cindy honestly.
description: Five pull-ups, ten push-ups, fifteen air squats, twenty minutes. How to pick a round pace you can hold, where rounds actually get lost, and how to scale Cindy honestly.

toc.title: What a Good Score Looks Like

bodyHtml:
What Cindy Is

Twenty minutes, as many rounds as possible: 5 pull-ups, 10 push-ups, 15 air squats. No barbell, no loading, nothing but a pull-up bar and enough floor space to lie down on. Cindy is one of the few benchmark workouts that fits into a hotel room, a garage, or a backyard with equal ease, which goes a long way toward explaining why it has outlasted most of what has been programmed alongside it.

Like Fran, it belongs to the original Girl WODs. Unlike Fran, it runs long enough that strategy compounds. Fran punishes a bad opening minute. Cindy punishes a bad opening five, then keeps punishing it for fifteen more.

Why Pacing Decides Your Score

Twenty minutes is long enough that almost nobody's limiting factor is strength. Twenty rounds works out to 100 pull-ups, 200 push-ups, and 300 air squats, and nobody has ever been stopped by the difficulty of a single air squat. What stops people is the push-up, and what breaks the push-up is going out too fast.

Round one takes most people somewhere around 45 seconds if they move without thinking about it. Hold that and you would finish 26 rounds. Almost nobody does, because a 45-second opening round means a 70-second round eight, and round fourteen spent face down on the mat doing push-ups one at a time.

The athletes who score well are usually the ones whose tenth round looks almost identical to their second.

"Your Cindy score is decided in the first five minutes, and almost always by going too fast in them."

Finding a Round Rhythm You Can Hold

Pick a target round time and hold it with a clock rather than by feel. One round per minute is the classic mark, and it is a sensible place to start because the math is trivial: twenty rounds in twenty minutes.

If a round takes you 50 seconds, you get 10 seconds of rest before the next one begins. That rest is the entire strategy. It is structured, it is predictable, and it keeps you from discovering at minute 12 that there is nothing left in the tank.

Stronger athletes run 45-second rounds and accept that they will slow down late. Newer athletes are usually better served by a 75 or 90 second round they can genuinely repeat twenty times. Either approach works. What does not work is having no target at all and letting fatigue set the pace for you.

Practical habit: Run five rounds at your intended pace as a warm-up on a normal training day. If round five feels harder than round two, the pace is too fast.

Where Rounds Actually Get Lost

Three places, roughly in order of how much they cost.

The push-ups come first. Ten is a small enough number that most people go unbroken for ten or twelve rounds, then hit a wall where the set becomes 6 and 4, then 4 and 3 and 3. Breaking them deliberately at 5 and 5 from round one feels absurdly conservative and usually produces a better final score.

The pull-ups come second, and they are mostly a grip problem. Five reps is nothing in isolation. Five reps a hundred times is a great deal of hanging. Drop off the bar the moment a set is finished instead of dangling there for an extra beat.

Transitions come third, and most people never think about them at all. Walking to the bar, chalking up, resetting your hands: three seconds a round is a full minute across twenty rounds, which is roughly a whole extra round left on the floor. Set your space up so the bar, your mat, and your squat spot are within a single step of each other.

Scaling Cindy So It Still Works

Cindy scales more gracefully than almost any other benchmark, because the only real requirement is that you keep moving for twenty minutes.

  • Jumping pull-ups: a box under the bar, one jump per rep. Keeps both the pace and the pulling pattern.
  • Inverted rows or banded rows: the right call if there is no bar you can hang from, or if five strict pull-ups are not there yet.
  • Hands elevated: put your hands on a box or a bench rather than dropping to your knees when you can. Elevated push-ups hold better positions and scale down smoothly as you get stronger.
  • Reduced reps: 3 pull-ups, 6 push-ups, 9 air squats keeps the ratio and the rhythm at roughly half the volume. A good option for a first attempt.

Whichever you pick, keep it constant for the full twenty minutes. Switching from pull-ups to jumping pull-ups at round eight makes the score impossible to compare against anything, including your own next attempt.

What a Good Score Looks Like

Twenty rounds, one per minute, is the number most people aim at and a genuinely strong result for an intermediate athlete. Fifteen rounds is solid. Ten rounds scaled, moving the whole time, is a good honest first Cindy and a far better starting point than a fast eight rounds followed by twelve minutes of standing around.

Past 25 rounds you are into serious territory. That is 125 pull-ups and 250 push-ups inside twenty minutes, and it tends to reflect years of gymnastics volume rather than a good day.

Final Thoughts

Cindy is the benchmark most worth repeating, because it asks for almost no equipment and still tells you something real. Run it every couple of months at the same scale with the same movements, and the trend line is about as honest a fitness measurement as you will get at home.

Set a round target before the clock starts. Break the push-ups earlier than feels necessary. Keep your gear within a step. And write the score down, because "somewhere around 16" is not a number you can improve on.

If you want a shorter bodyweight piece for the days between benchmarks, the WOD Builder will build one around whatever you have on hand.
